Neonatal calves of the long-finned pilot whale emerge at a body length of approximately 177 centimeters [Lb = approximately 177 centimeters], a size that facilitates successful suckling and thermoregulation in cold North Atlantic waters. The corresponding wet weight at birth is around 75 kilograms [Wwb = around 75 kilograms], reflecting the substantial maternal investment characteristic of this deep-diving delphinid. Field studies conducted over several decades have recorded that the gestation period, measured at the core body temperature typical of cetaceans (37 °C [T = 37 °C]), spans about 450 days [tg = about 450 days]. This extended gestation is consistent with the general pattern among globicephalines, where prolonged uterine development results in a precocial calf capable of swimming alongside its mother within hours of delivery. Comparisons with the closely related short-finned pilot whale indicate that the birth length of Globicephala melas is slightly larger, likely an adaptation to the cooler, more productive foraging grounds it occupies. The high degree of maternal care required after parturition underscores the slow life-history strategy that typifies this species.

Considerable sexual dimorphism exists in the ultimate body size attained by adult long-finned pilot whales. Females reach a maximum recorded length of approximately 460 centimeters [Li = approximately 460 centimeters], whereas males can grow substantially larger, achieving an ultimate length of about 600 centimeters [Li = about 600 centimeters]. This pronounced disparity in size, with males often exceeding females by over a meter, is among the most extreme observed within the family Delphinidae. The corresponding ultimate wet weight for females is around 1100 kilograms [Wwi = around 1100 kilograms], while males attain a much greater body mass of approximately 2320 kilograms [Wwi = approximately 2320 kilograms]. Such dimorphism is thought to be linked to the species' polygynous mating system, where larger males are more successful in intra-sexual competition for access to receptive females. Growth curves derived from long-term photo-identification studies indicate that asymptotic body size is not reached until well into the second decade of life, a reflection of the species' extended developmental period. These size differences also influence diving capacity and foraging behavior between the sexes.

The onset of reproductive maturity in this species occurs at different body sizes for males and females, a pattern documented through extensive necropsy and life-history data. Females attain puberty at a body length of approximately 374.5 centimeters [Lp = approximately 374.5 centimeters], with the corresponding wet weight at puberty for females recorded at roughly 607.3 kilograms [Wwp = roughly 607.3 kilograms]. Males, in contrast, reach sexual maturity at a distinctly larger size, with a length at puberty of about 470 centimeters [Lp = about 470 centimeters] and a wet weight at puberty for males of around 1100 kilograms [Wwp = around 1100 kilograms]. The time since birth at which this developmental milestone is reached, measured at the typical mammalian body temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C], differs notably between the sexes. Females achieve sexual maturity at approximately 8.1 years [tp = approximately 8.1 years] at a temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C] of age. Males follow a slower trajectory, reaching puberty at around 4380 days after birth [tp = around 4380 days after birth], a delay of several years that reflects their extended growth period required to attain the massive body size characteristic of breedin at a temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C]g males. This pattern of delayed male maturity is common among highly dimorphic marine mammals.

Reproductive output in long-finned pilot whales is remarkably low, consistent with a K-selected life-history strategy typical of long-lived cetaceans. Females produce a single calf per litter at a maximum frequency of one litter every five years, yielding a maximum reproductive rate of 0.2 calves per year [Ri = 0.2 calves per year]. This exceptionally low rate, calculated at the species' core body temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C], is among the lowest recorded for any delphinid. The time since birth at weaning, also measured at 37 °C [T = 37 °C], lasts approximately 812 days [tx = approximately 812 days], a prolonged period of nutritional dependency that allows the calf to learn complex foraging techniques, including coordinated deep-diving and prey capture. During this extended nursing phase, the mother bears a considerable energetic cost, and the interval between successive births is consequently prolonged. Life-history models suggest that such a slow reproductive schedule is viable only because of the species' exceptional longevity and high adult survival rates. Comparative studies indicate that pilot whales have a lower reproductive rate than many other similarly sized toothed whales.

Long-finned pilot whales are among the longest-lived delphinids, with a documented maximum lifespan of approximately 60 years [am = approximately 60 years] at a core body temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C]. This exceptional longevity, combined with a delayed age at first reproduction and a low annual reproductive output, places the species at the extreme slow end of the mammalian life-history continuum. Analyses of tooth growth layers in stranded individuals from the Faroe Islands have confirmed that females can remain reproductively active well into their fourth decade, with some individuals exhibiting signs of reproductive senescence only after age 50. The species' slow pace of life is thought to be an evolutionary response to the unpredictable distribution of their primary prey, which includes squid and demersal fish in deep, offshore waters. Social structure plays a crucial role in this longevity, as pilot whales live in stable, matrilineal pods where older females act as repositories of ecological knowledge, guiding younger pod members to productive foraging grounds. This post-reproductive lifespan, a rare phenomenon among mammals, further emphasizes the species' deeply social and slow-living life-history strategy. Ongoing research continues to investigate the genetic and physiological mechanisms underlying their remarkable resistance to age-related diseases.
